Fixing the bug where wrong cpu label values were getting assigned to the samples (#3148)

Bug: 
When viewing the data collected from the agent as flamechart, samples
grouped by node + cpu, there were overlapping stacks, which cannot
happen ideally.

Root cause: 
The labels lru cache in the `parca-reporter` is only using tid as the
cache key and when a thread gets scheduled across different cpu cores
across the profiling ticks, we only use the labels cached from the first
occurrence of the tid.
So, if the tid when first seen was on cpu `1`, then it gets reported the
same for all future occurrences, even though it can be seen on a
different cpu core.

Fix:
Made `pid` the label cache key and patching cpu, thread_id and
thread_name labels on the fly. This reduced the memory footprint of this
cache as well.

Flags:
Added 3 more flags to control these labels, as they don't belong to the
relabeling path anymore:
- `--metadata-disable-cpu-label`
- `--metadata-disable-thread-id-label`
- `--metadata-disable-thread-comm-label`

The CRI client fast path (cri_client.go:convertSandboxToPod) sets

fix: handle bare container IDs from CRI client in matchContainerID (#3157)

## Summary

- Make `containerIDPattern` regex accept both prefixed
(`containerd://hex`) and bare (`hex`) 64-char container IDs
- Downgrade `log.Error` to `log.Debugf` in `getKubernetesPodMetadata` to
match the level used in `addPodContainerLabels` for the same error
- Add unit tests for `matchContainerID` covering both formats and edge
cases

## Problem

The CRI client fast path (`cri_client.go:convertSandboxToPod`) sets
`ContainerStatus.ContainerID` to the bare runtime ID from the CRI API
(`container.Id`), which is a 64-char hex string without the
`containerd://` prefix. The kubelet normally adds this prefix when
constructing `ContainerStatus` for the Kubernetes API, but the CRI
client bypasses the kubelet.

The `containerIDPattern` regex (`.+://([0-9a-f]{64})`) requires the
`://` prefix, so every CRI-sourced container lookup fails. Combined with
`log.Error` level logging, this generates N_processes * M_containers
error logs per profiling cycle - over 10,000 logs/hour across our fleet
of 134 agents.

## Fix

**Commit 1** - Regex: `.+://([0-9a-f]{64})` to
`^(?:.+://)?([0-9a-f]{64})$`
- `^...$` anchors prevent substring matching (stricter than original)
- `(?:.+://)?` makes the prefix optional
- Handles both Kubernetes API format and CRI API format

**Commit 2** - Log level: `log.Error` to `log.Debugf` in
`getKubernetesPodMetadata`
- The function does a linear scan over all containers to find the one
matching a PID
- Non-matching containers are expected, not errors
- Matches the level already used in `addPodContainerLabels` for the same
error

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests for `matchContainerID` covering prefixed IDs, bare IDs,
and invalid inputs (empty, short, non-hex, 65 chars, cgroup paths,
trailing chars)
- [x] Regex verified against live GKE 1.32 cluster ContainerID values

fix: avoid nil dereference in symbol uploader when temp file creation fails

When os.Create fails in attemptUpload, f is nil. The error handler
called os.Remove(f.Name()), which panics with a nil pointer
dereference. Remove the call — there is no file to clean up when
creation fails, and the defer on the success path already handles it.

fix: avoid nil dereference in symbol uploader when temp file creation fails (#3163)

`attemptUpload` creates a temporary file before extracting debuginfo. If
`os.Create` fails, the current error path calls `os.Remove(f.Name())`,
but `f`
is `nil` in that case, so `f.Name()` panics and crashes the agent.

I ran into this on a NixOS host after parca-agent panicked in the symbol
uploader while processing a wrapper binary under `/run/wrappers/...`.
The
stack trace pointed back to the `os.Create` error path in
`reporter/parca_uploader.go`.

This change removes the `os.Remove(f.Name())` call from the `os.Create`
error
branch. When file creation fails, there is no file to remove, and the
function
now returns the original `create file` error instead of panicking.

gpu: GPU PC sampling support in the agent (#3184)

Adds GPU profiling driven by parcagpu's CUPTI shim. The agent attaches to
the shim's USDT probes, receives per-pid GpuConfig (sampling factor,
clock_khz, SM count) from the cuda_gpu_config probe, and reports two GPU
views as Parca sample types.

Reporting model (non-merged, the default):

  gpu_kernel_time / nanoseconds   exact kernel durations (CUDA callbacks)
  gpu_pcsample    / count         PC samples — all PC activity, not just
                                  stalls; value is the raw sample count,
                                  period = NsPerSample = 2^SamplingFactor
                                  / clock_hz, so value × period totals ns

PC sampling observes all PC activity (normally scheduled instructions as
well as stalls), so it is reported as a count of samples with a per-sample
time weight in the period — mirroring CPU sampling (samples/count :
cpu/nanoseconds) — rather than as a pre-converted "stall time". The count
stays correct even if a sample arrives before its GpuConfig probe; only
the period is unknown until the config event lands (one-shot warn per pid
via gpu.WarnMissingGpuConfig).

MergeGpuProfiles (default false) opts into a single gpu_time/nanoseconds
sample type that folds both views together, differentiated by a gpu_view
label (kernel_time|pc_sample); there the PC count is converted to ns
inline.

* reporter: add ParcaReporter log-event interface and per-sample relabel

Introduce a reporter.ParcaReporter interface that extends otel's
TraceReporter with Logger(scope string) log.Logger so any producer
(uprobes or otherwise) can ship OTel log records through a shared gRPC
connection without owning its own pipeline.

The existing struct is renamed arrowReporter and now owns a
*sdklog.LoggerProvider built from:
  - go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploggrpc as the
    transport, configured with WithGRPCConn so it shares the connection
    already established for profile data;
  - sdklog.NewBatchProcessor for queue + batch + retry (size 512, age
    250ms, queue depth 4096), tuned tighter than the SDK default so

probes: BPF uprobe service for entry/exit duration tracking via OTLP logs (#3181)

## Summary

Adds a generic eBPF uprobe service that attaches paired entry/exit
probes to declared symbols and emits per-call duration records through
the OTLP logs pipeline introduced in #3190.

The motivating use case is finding long JS execution blocks in Node.js
applications. A 200 ms callback hogging the libuv event loop is exactly
the "phantom" tail latency that doesn't show up in CPU profiles. The
reference config attaches to `node::InternalCallbackScope`'s ctor +
dtor, brackets each outer libuv callback, and emits one record per scope
close with a precise duration measured in BPF.

## What's added

- **`probes/` package**:
- YAML config schema: `{id, file_match (regex), entry_symbol,
exit_symbol, main_thread_only, min_duration_ms}`.
- eBPF uprobe program (paired entry + exit) with a per-tid scope counter
that emits only when the outer scope closes. Nested scopes roll into the
outer's measured duration. Main-thread filter via `tid == tgid` directly
in BPF; libuv worker-pool / V8 background threads are silently dropped.
- User-space drains the BPF ringbuf and emits one OTel `log.Record` per
completed outer scope via `Logger("parca-agent.probes")`, so consumers
can filter on `attributes_scope.name` to slice probe records vs other
agent logs.
- **`--probe-config <path>`** CLI flag (default: disabled). Requires a
remote-store.
- **Reference `probes/testdata/probes.yaml.sample`** with the Node.js
`InternalCallbackScope` ctor + dtor pair pre-verified on Node v18.20 /
v22.17 / v24.4 (same mangled symbol on all three, exported via `.dynsym`
so stripped builds work too).
- **Build system**: single arch-agnostic `probe.bpf.o` (no `PT_REGS_*`
macros used). `Makefile` + `.goreleaser.yml` `before:` hook + CI
workflow + `probes/bpf/README.md` set up to produce it on every release.

## Data on the wire

Each probe-fire record:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `body` | `"node.callback_scope"` (stable; queryable) |
| `timestamp` | exit ktime → unix ns via shared `times.KTime` offset
(aligned with CPU sample timestamps; range queries over `[start_ns,
end_ns]` against the profile-samples table don't drift) |
| `attributes` | `start_ns`, `end_ns`, `duration_ns`, `pid`, `tid`,
`comm`, `is_main`, `spec_id`, `probe_id`, `level` |
| `resource` | inherited from the OTel SDK `LoggerProvider`:
`service.name`, `service.version`, `host.name` |
| `scope` | `"parca-agent.probes"` |

reporter: split memory traces onto a dedicated ParcaReporter.ReportMemoryTraces path

Memory profiles used to ride on the otel TraceReporter contract: the
oomprof adapter built a fake libpf.Trace per sample, stuffed alloc/free
counters onto it via a synthetic MemoryPayloadFrame, and called
ReportTraceEvent. That worked but pushed memory-specific shape into the
otel-facing trace interface and burned one writer-lock acquisition per
sample.

Memory profiling upstream is evolving in a different direction and we
want to reduce fork drift so this greases the skids for the future.

  * `ParcaReporter` is now an interface (reporter/iface.go) embedding
    the otel `reporter.Reporter` + `ExecutableReporter` and adding
    `ReportMetrics` and the new `ReportMemoryTraces(samples, meta)`.
  * The concrete struct is renamed `arrowReporter`; `New(...)` returns
    the interface.
  * `arrowReporter.ReportMemoryTraces` writes memory rows v2-only,
    computes labels once per batch, takes the v2 writer lock once,
    and emits 2-4 rows (inuse_objects / inuse_space and, when
    enabled, alloc_objects / alloc_space) per sample.
  * The oomprof callback is wired through a new `oomprofAdapter`
    (reporter/oomprof_adapter.go) that implements `oomprof.Reporter`,
    chunks incoming batches into groups of 100, and forwards each
    chunk to `ReportMemoryTraces`.

That lets us delete:

  * `extractMemoryPayload` and its callers in `ReportTraceEvent`
    (the synthetic-payload-frame side channel).
  * The `oomprofMemoryFrame = 0xFF` shim plus its `case` in the
    v1 stacktrace builder and the v2 location builder.
  * The v1 and v2 `case TraceOriginMemory:` branches in
    `reportTraceEvent` / `reportTraceEventV2` (memory no longer
    flows through there).
  * `SampleEvents` on the concrete reporter, now replaced by the
    adapter.

Bonus: the v2 memory path now actually increments `r.memorySamples`
(the previous code only incremented it on the dead v1 branch).

No `main.go` source edits are required — the interface return from
`reporter.New` covers `Start`, `Stop`, `ReportTraceEvent`,
`ReportExecutable`, `ReportMetrics`, and the new
`ReportMemoryTraces`, satisfying every consumer (tracer, metrics,
parcagpu).

The Artifacts workflow runs in `goreleaser/goreleaser-cross:v1.22.4`,

Worth noting for anyone who saw this and assumed an expiry: the
`Release` files are **not** expired and `apt-get update` succeeds. The
indices are still served — only the `.deb` pool files under
`debian-security` have been removed. That combination is what archival
looks like partway through.

## Fix

Bump the container to `v1.27.1`.

goreleaser-cross **v1.26.5 and later** build on `ubuntu:noble` (via
`goreleaser-cross-toolchains` v0.1.9). I checked that image still
provides everything the build depends on:

- `clang` and `llvm` — needed by the `make probes-bpf` hook that runs
before goreleaser builds
- `crossbuild-essential-amd64` / `crossbuild-essential-arm64` — so
`CC=x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc` and `CC=aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` in
`.goreleaser.yml` still resolve
- a much newer `libbpf-dev` than bullseye's 0.3

`gcc -print-multiarch` behaves the same on Ubuntu, so the Makefile's
`BPF_CFLAGS` multiarch include path still resolves.

### Why bump rather than pin to archive.debian.org

Repointing apt at `archive.debian.org` would have been a smaller diff,
but it keeps release builds on an EOL base image that receives no
security updates, against a libbpf from 2021. That trades a visible
breakage for an invisible one.

### Release binaries are unaffected

The glibc jump (2.31 → 2.39) does not reach users: `.goreleaser.yml`
sets `CGO_ENABLED=1` but builds with `-extldflags=-static` and the
`osusergo`/`netgo` tags, so the binaries are fully static and nothing
links against the builder's glibc at runtime.

ci: resolve snap binary paths by build ID, not hardcoded suffix (#3217)

## Problem

Follow-up to #3216 — that PR fixed the archived-bullseye apt failure,
but moving to a newer goreleaser changed the `dist/` layout and broke
the snap job:

```
cp: cannot stat './dist/linux-arm64_linux_arm64/parca-agent': No such file or directory
```

goreleaser suffixes each build directory with the microarchitecture
level it targeted, and the `GOARM64` default gained an explicit one:

```
dist/linux-amd64_linux_amd64_v1      (unchanged)
dist/linux-arm64_linux_arm64_v8.0    (was: linux-arm64_linux_arm64)
```

amd64 was unaffected because it already carried the `GOAMD64` `_v1`
suffix, which is why only the arm64 copy failed.

## Fix

Glob on the build ID prefix rather than hardcoding the suffix, so the
default can shift again without breaking the job.

Also added an explicit check that each arch matched exactly once.
Without it a future rename shows up as a bare `cp` ENOENT with no
context, which is what made this one slower to diagnose than it needed
to be — now it prints what it matched and lists `dist/`. The check also
guards the worse failure mode: if a stale binary were left in
`snap/local/` from the preceding amd64 step, a silently-failing copy
would pack the wrong architecture rather than erroring.

## Testing

I verified the glob logic directly against reconstructed directory
layouts:

- new layout (`linux-arm64_linux_arm64_v8.0`) → resolves
- old layout (`linux-arm64_linux_arm64`) → still resolves, so this is
not coupled to the current goreleaser version
- missing arm64 build → fails with the diagnostic and a non-zero exit,
rather than proceeding

The snap job on this PR is the end-to-end check.

## Note on the prior state

Worth recording: the snap job was **not** previously passing either —
the last green Artifacts run on `main` was 2026-08-24. The 2026-08-26
run failed earlier, during `Goreleaser release`, on an unrelated
`gojsontoyaml` sumdb error, so the arm64 path had not been exercised in
a while. #3216 got the workflow far enough to reach this.

Bump ebpf-profiler fork to e2457aba (#3215)

Picks up four GPU/USDT fixes from the fork. All are merged, so this pins
the fork's `main` rather than a branch tip.

## What this fixes

**Cubins could not be parsed at all**
([#329](https://github.com/parca-dev/opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler/pull/329)).
NVIDIA stores a toolkit-specific value in the 32-bit `e_version` field,
which `debug/elf` rejects outright. CUDA 12.9
(`nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.06-py3`) writes 129:

```
failed to parse cubin ELF (crc=0x9a98f5ca): parse cubin ELF:
mismatched ELF version 'EV_CURRENT+128' in record at byte 0x0
```

**Cubin debug files were never uploaded**
([#331](https://github.com/parca-dev/opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler/pull/331)).
#329 fixed only `ParseCubinELF`; `cubinProcess.OpenMappingFile` still
handed out raw bytes, so our symbol uploader hit the same rejection and
GPU frames stayed unsymbolized:

```
Failed to upload with fileName 'cubin-000000000ee1858b' and buildID '':
extract debuginfo: initialize nullifying writer: error reading ELF file:
mismatched ELF version 'EV_CURRENT+128' in record at byte 0x0
```

**PC samples had stall reasons but no instruction mnemonics**
([#332](https://github.com/parca-dev/opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler/pull/332)),
on every pre-Blackwell GPU. The SM version was read from `e_flags` bits
`[8:15]`, which only holds it from Blackwell on — up to sm_90 it is the
low byte, and those bits are feature flags. A typical sm_90 cubin
decoded as 5, so no SASS opcode table matched and every mnemonic came
back empty. Silently, since 5 is nonzero and passed the existing guard.

**USDT attachment broke and never recovered**
([#330](https://github.com/parca-dev/opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler/pull/330)).
Spec map entries were leaked on nearly every attach path; once
`__bpf_usdt_specs` fills, further attaches fail with `E2BIG`, which
cilium/ebpf surfaces as the misleading `"key too big for map"`:

```
Failed to handle new interpreter for PID ... file /var/lib/parca/gpu/libparcagpucupti.so:
... failed to populate USDT spec maps: store spec for parcagpu:cuda_correlation:
update: key too big for map: argument list too long
```

At 7 probes per process for `libparcagpucupti.so`, GPU nodes hit this
quickly.

These interacted on the same nodes, which made the logs confusing to
read: with the spec map exhausted, `cubin_loaded` rarely attached, so
the cubin parse failure only became visible at volume after a restart
cleared the map.

## Diff

`go.mod` + `go.sum` only:

```
-replace go.opentelemetry.io/ebpf-profiler => github.com/parca-dev/opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler v0.0.0-20260821130017-2a9d871a7e3a
+replace go.opentelemetry.io/ebpf-profiler => github.com/parca-dev/opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler v0.0.202637-0.20260915133107-e2457aba2d5e
```

`go mod tidy` also reclassified `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/metric` from
direct to indirect — unrelated to this bump, nothing in the tree imports
it directly, so it was a stale entry tidy corrected.

`cilium/ebpf` is unchanged at v0.22.0, so no bpf2go wrapper regeneration
is needed.

## Testing

I verified the resolved module actually contains all four fixes rather
than inferring it from the SHA. All profiler-consuming packages
(`parcagpu`, `reporter`, `metrics`, `oom`) build and their tests compile
clean for `linux/amd64`.

**Not verified on real GPU hardware.** Two things worth watching after
this deploys:

- the `[cuda] cubin loaded: crc=... sm=%d texts=%d` debug line should
now read `sm=90` on an H100 rather than `sm=5`, and
`cuda_sass_instruction` labels should appear alongside
`cuda_stall_reason`
- whether the uploaded cubin debug files actually symbolize —
`GnuBuildID` is deliberately empty and the uploader falls back to
`BUILD_ID_TYPE_HASH`, which none of this has exercised end to end

## Follow-up

`__bpf_usdt_specs` has `max_entries` 256, which covers only ~36
concurrent CUDA processes even with zero leaks. A bump to 2048 is ready
but needs the committed `tracer.ebpf.{amd64,arm64}` blobs regenerated in
the pinned dev container, so it is not in this change.

Fix CVE-2026-39821 and other advisories for v0.49.1 (#3210)

Google Cloud Marketplace flagged our published images for CVE-2026-39821
(GO-2026-5026), a Punycode validation flaw in golang.org/x/net/idna
where ToASCII/ToUnicode accept an encoded label that decodes to an
ASCII-only one, letting it slip past a hostname privilege check.

The x/net module was already on v0.56.0, which carries the fix, so this
looked like a false positive at first. It isn't: idna is also vendored
into the standard library, and v0.49.0 was built with go1.25.11.
govulncheck on the published binary still reports GO-2026-5026 reachable
through net/http. The stdlib fix landed in go1.25.13, so raise the go
directive to require it -- CI resolves go-version '~1.25' to the latest
patch anyway, but nothing was stopping an older toolchain from producing
a vulnerable build.

That clears seven further stdlib advisories that came along for the
ride. containerd v1.7.33 is a patch bump and clears two more.
Deliberately
left alone: cilium/ebpf, grpc and prometheus all need minor-version
jumps
into core profiling paths, which is not what a security patch release is
for.

govulncheck on the resulting binary: 21 findings down to 11, none of
them
in the standard library, and GO-2026-5026 gone.

metadata: report which cgroup hierarchy ID failed to parse

parseCgroupString formatted the parsed hierarchy ID with %q on the error path.
It is an int, so %q renders it as a rune literal rather than a quoted string,
and on that path it is always the zero value strconv.Atoi returned -- so every
malformed line produced the same "hierarchy ID: '\x00'", naming neither the
input nor the cause. go vet is quiet about it because %q is a legal verb for
integers.

Print the offending field and wrap the strconv error, which makes the message
"invalid hierarchy ID \"abc\": strconv.Atoi: parsing \"abc\": invalid syntax"
and leaves errors.Is matching ErrFileParse as before. The function had no
tests, so this adds them for both cgroup versions and both parse failures.

metadata: fix %q on an int that Go 1.26 vet now rejects (#3220)

`go test ./reporter/metadata/` fails to build on `main` since the Go
1.26 bump (#3218):

```
reporter/metadata/process.go:69:45: fmt.Errorf format %q has arg cgroup.hierarchyID of wrong type int
```

Go 1.26's vet rejects `%q` on an integer, which earlier versions
accepted (it renders as a rune literal).

## The bug it was hiding

```go
cgroup.hierarchyID, err = strconv.Atoi(fields[0])
if err != nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: hierarchy ID: %q", ErrFileParse, cgroup.hierarchyID)
}
```

Besides the wrong verb, the value is wrong: on the error path
`hierarchyID` is always the zero value `strconv.Atoi` returned. Every
malformed line in `/proc/[pid]/cgroup` produced the same message, naming
neither the offending input nor the cause:

```
Error Parsing File: hierarchy ID: '\x00'
```

## The fix

Print the field that failed and wrap the `strconv` error:

```
Error Parsing File: invalid hierarchy ID "abc": strconv.Atoi: parsing "abc": invalid syntax
```

`errors.Is(err, ErrFileParse)` still matches, and now `errors.Is(err,
strconv.ErrSyntax)` does too.

The function had no tests, so this adds them: both cgroup versions, a
path containing colons, and both parse failures. The non-numeric case
asserts the message quotes the input and no longer contains `\x00`.

reporter: add OTLP/profiles as a third export format

Selected with --remote-store-format=otlp, alongside the existing arrow v1 and
v2 paths. Verified end to end against two independent OTLP/profiles receivers,
both rendering symbolized flamegraphs from the agent's output.

The conversion is ours rather than upstream's. Upstream's lives in
reporter/internal/pdata, which is unimportable, and no extension point would
have helped: pprofile.Profile carries exactly one SampleType, so a memory
profile with four value axes needs four Profiles, and oomprof never passes
through an origin at all; baseReporter also rejects the CUDA and GPU-PC origins
before the encoding is reached. Owning it means every origin the tracer
produces has a sample type, including GPU and memory.

reporter/pprofile.go builds one Profiles per flush with a request-global
dictionary, partitioning into Profiles by (sample type, unit, period type,
period) so GPU-PC's per-PID period lands on its own Profile. It reserves
mapping index 0 as the "no mapping" sentinel, because Location.MappingIndex has
no presence flag. Memory frames get a special case: ReportMemoryTraces stashes
the build ID in FunctionName and the executable path in SourceFile, which a
generic classifier would emit as a function literally named after a build ID.

Flags:

  --remote-store-format gains otlp. All three formats ride the existing
  remote-store connection, so OTLP inherits its TLS, auth, retry and client
  metrics rather than opening a second one.

  --remote-store-compression=gzip|none applies to the OTLP export only; the
  arrow paths compress inside their own IPC payload. gzip at level 1 rather
  than the level-6 default, since the CPU is spent on a node being profiled:
  level 1 runs at 192 MB/s against level 6's 108 MB/s for 6.6% of the ratio.
  gzip is the only choice because it is the only codec grpc-go ships on both
  sides; anything else fails at the first flush against a receiver that did
  not install it, which is not worth trading for a better ratio on a stream
  that runs at tens of KiB/s.

  --debuginfo-address points symbol upload at its own host, inheriting the
  remote store's credentials. Symbols travel the DebuginfoService protocol
  whatever encoding profiles use, so OTLP mode is not standalone, and flag
  validation says so rather than failing at the first upload.

Also fixed here:

  service.name was set only from APMServiceName, so a system-wide profiler
  sent anonymous resources for nearly everything and consumers keying on it
  named every process by a hash. Now falls back to comm, then the executable's
  basename.

  The remote store was dialed whenever the agent was not in offline mode, which
  was right when "not offline" implied "has a remote store".
  --remote-store-format=otlp with --debuginfo-upload-disable and no address is a
  third case, and it died on "received empty target in Build()". The dial is now
  gated on a non-empty address, which also makes the OTLP path's grpcConn == nil
  check reachable instead of dead.

Known gaps: OTLP has no field for aggregation temporality, so a consumer must
derive delta from the sample type; off-CPU is wallclock on arrow and off_cpu on
OTLP, which is still an open naming decision; and offline mode has no OTLP
representation and is rejected at flag validation.

main: add --symbolize-go to resolve Go frames in the agent

The upstream Go interpreter reads gopclntab out of the binary and resolves
function, file and line in-agent. It was unconditionally disabled with no way
to turn it on, because Parca symbolizes native Go frames server-side from
uploaded debuginfo and doing it in both places pays for the same answer twice.

That reasoning holds only when the backend has a symbolizer. Against one that
does not, Go frames arrive as bare addresses and nothing later can name them,
since the agent is the only place gopclntab was available.

Off by default, so nothing changes for a Parca backend. On, it costs agent CPU
and memory per Go process and needs no debuginfo upload at all.

Independent of the profile encoding: it works the same on every
--remote-store-format.

reporter: only build the self-logs provider when logs are exported

non-nil, which is every non-offline run. --otlp-logging only controlled
whether main.go attached the logrus hook to the other end, so the usual

It is not free. The processor allocates on its own timer regardless of

span is created, and the probe service needs the one it gets today.

allocation profiles over 60s: with --otlp-logging the clone appears at
65.6 MiB, 6.3% of bytes; without it, no log.Record allocation at all.

reporter: benchmark both encoders against a null gRPC endpoint

Whole-agent measurements could not answer which encoder is cheaper. Under a
realistic workload the agent's allocation profile is 45-53% eh_frame
extraction, so an encoder difference of any plausible size is inside the
noise, and the run-to-run variance in how many new executables a window
happens to discover is larger than the effect being looked for.

These benchmarks remove everything except the reporter. A .padata file named
by PARCA_BENCH_CORPUS is decoded back into the ReportTraceEvent arguments
that produced it, once, outside the timer; the benchmark replays them. With
no corpus set the benchmarks skip, so `go test ./...` stays hermetic.

The endpoint is a bufconn server with a raw codec and an unknown-service
handler: it accepts any method, decodes nothing, and replies with an empty
message. That detail is load-bearing. Registering the generated services
instead charges the benchmark for the receiver's unmarshal, which is wildly
asymmetric -- an arrow request is one bytes field, an OTLP request rebuilds
every Sample, Stack and Location in pdata. It inflated OTLP by 41%
(603,699 allocs/op against the 356,951 the agent actually pays) before the
codec was swapped in. The client side stays real: real codec, real
compression, real HTTP/2 framing.

Two pairs of benchmarks. Encode* is a whole flush interval, accumulate plus
serialize plus send. *Accumulate drops the flush, so the difference between
them is what serialization costs.

Reconstruction is faithful except for FileID: the arrow schema stores a
mapping as (filename, build ID) and keeps no FileID, so one is synthesized by
hashing that pair. The encoders use it as a dictionary key and as the htlhash
build-ID fallback, both of which only need stability and distinctness, so
cardinality is right even though the values are not real.
TestBenchCorpusSanity guards the decode -- an off-by-one in the ListView
offsets would produce empty stacks, which would benchmark nothing and look
fast doing it.

reporter: append a stack's location indices in one call

internStack appended one location index per frame. Every Append on an empty
Int32Slice regrows the backing array from zero, and at a mean stack depth of
33 that made pcommon.Int32Slice.Append the single largest allocator in the
whole OTLP encode path -- 1.44M objects, 12.3% of everything allocated during
accumulation, ahead of every pdata constructor.

Collect the indices in a scratch slice reused across stacks, size the
destination once, and append them together. The scratch is never aliased by
the dictionary, which copies on Append.

Measured with BenchmarkEncodeOTLP over a 20,000-sample corpus, 33.1 frames
per sample, 231 PIDs, 83 mappings:

  allocs/op   356,951 -> 289,561   (-19%)
  B/op         31.9MB ->  28.5MB   (-10%)
  ns/op         167.6 ->   159.1   (-5%)

It does not close the gap to arrow v2, which is still about 1.6x cheaper on
this corpus, but it is the largest single item and the cheapest to fix.

reporter: format per-sample label values with strconv, not fmt.Sprint

labelsForTID formats a CPU number and a thread ID on every sample, on the path
both backends take. fmt.Sprint boxes each argument into an interface and goes
through the reflection formatter; strconv.FormatUint does neither, and returns
a shared string with no allocation at all for values below 100.

Over 20,000 samples per iteration, 3 runs of 8: 30,140 allocations removed from
each backend, -10% for OTLP and -23% for arrow v2, which allocates less to
begin with. Wall time moves about 2%.

A lookup table for larger values was tried and removed: it measured identically,
because strconv already has the small-value fast path and thread IDs are mostly
too large for any table worth keeping.

reporter: emit thread.id and cpu.logical_number as integers

Both are integers in the semantic conventions and in upstream's OTLP reporter,
which appends them with AppendInt. Ours went out as strings, because
appendAttr only ever calls Value().SetStr and the per-sample values reach the
builder as Prometheus label strings. A consumer that reads thread.id as an int
either errors or drops the attribute, and nothing about the profile looks
wrong when it does.

appendIntAttr writes the typed value; appendParsedIntAttr converts what the
label pipeline already formatted. The round trip is the cost of routing
per-sample values through Prometheus labels for the arrow writers, and it goes
away if enrichment ever produces typed attributes directly. A value that will
not parse ships as a string rather than being dropped, since a relabel rule
can rewrite these names.

attrKey gains an isInt discriminator. Without it a string "42" and an integer
42 share a cache slot and whichever is interned first decides the type for
both.

Also stamps SchemaUrl on ResourceProfiles and ScopeProfiles, which upstream
sets and we omitted. It is spelled out rather than taken from the semconv
module, for the same reason the attribute keys are: a module bump must not
silently change what a consumer thinks it is reading.

Arrow output is untouched; none of this is on that path.

reporter: give the per-sample labels their own factory

cpu, thread_id and thread_name change from sample to sample within one
process, so they cannot come from the per-PID metadata providers or ride in
processLabeler's cache. Three separate places knew that: labelsForTID built
them inline from three disable flags, perSampleLabelNames listed them again so
the probe relabel pass could split them back out, and AddSample switched on
their names a third time to map them onto semconv attributes and decide which
two are integers. Adding a fourth per-sample label meant finding all three.

sampleLabeler owns them now. sampleLabelSpecs is one row per label carrying
the Prometheus name the arrow writers column on, the OTLP attribute key, and
whether that attribute is typed as an integer; build, split and the builder's
attribute mapping all read from it. Both backends share it: arrow keeps
flattening the label set through labelRetrievalResult.forEach and needs no
change at all, while the OTLP builder looks a name up instead of switching on
it.

The carrier stays labels.Labels rather than a typed struct. A per-sample
relabel pass can rewrite these values, so the OTLP side has to work from names
regardless, and a typed fast path would mean two sources of truth for one
attribute. The cost is the ParseInt that appendParsedIntAttr already noted.

No behaviour change. Relabelling still skips the per-sample labels on the
CPU/off-CPU/memory/GPU paths and still runs the merged pass for probes.

resolveAttrs in the pprofile tests now reads values with AsString rather than
Str. It has been reading the integer attributes back as empty since fe163ffa
made them integers, so TestPprofileAttributeSplit was asserting cpu == "3"
against "" and failing.

## What changed upstream

**#1576 replaced `TraceEventMeta.Origin` with
`TraceEventMeta.ProfileType`.** `Origin` was a small enum
(`support.TraceOriginSampling` and friends); `ProfileType` is a
`*samples.TypeMetadata` carrying the profile's period and sample type
strings. Both reporters and `parcagpu` switched on `Origin`, so they all
move over.

**#1564 folded the standalone `labels` interpreter into Go**, so
`interpreterconfig.Labels` no longer exists.

## Matching on SampleType rather than pointer identity

The profiler registers one `TypeMetadata` per kind at load time and
hands that same pointer back on every event, so comparing pointers is
the obvious way to tell kinds apart. It isn't available to us: sampling,
off-CPU and probe are declared as anonymous literals at their
registration sites, and `originRegistry` exposes only the `uint16` ID.
There is no way for a downstream reporter to name them.

That's deliberate rather than an oversight — upstream's own converter
never asks which kind a sample is, it just copies the metadata's fields
into the profile. Upstream has since moved off-CPU and probe out of the
tracer entirely, into `probes/offcpu` and `probes/uprobe`, where each
plugin registers its own literal in `Load()`. So this isn't going to
change, and a package-level `ProfileTypeOffCPU` var in the fork would
silently stop matching the moment that restructure lands in a merge
stack.

`SampleType` is unique across all five kinds we handle (`samples`,
`off_cpu`, `events`, `gpu_kernel_time`, `gpu_pcsample`), it survives the
restructure, and nothing in either repo assigns to a `TypeMetadata`
field after construction. `reporter/profiletypes.go` holds the constants
and the reasoning.

### The weakness, stated plainly

Nothing ties our strings to upstream's, so an upstream rename of
`off_cpu` would land as samples falling through to the `default` case.
Each switch logs there.

Two of the five can be anchored: `interpreter/gpu` exports its profile
types, so `TestGPUSampleTypeConstantsMatchProfiler` asserts our
constants against the metadata the profiler actually registers, rather
than against a copy. `TestOTLPReporterEveryProfileTypeIsExportable/cuda`
catches a mismatch too, since it feeds the genuine `gpu.ProfileTypeCuda`
pointer end to end. The three tracer-owned kinds have no such anchor;
tests rebuild them field for field.

An earlier attempt exported the three from the fork instead. It was
dropped — upstream won't take it (anonymous is the design), and it
breaks silently on the probes restructure, which is a worse failure than
a rename we'd at least see in the logs.

## `--tracers=labels`

`cfg.Labels` is gone. The flag now sets `cfg.Go.Labels` **and**
`cfg.CustomLabels`. Both halves matter: `CustomLabels` gates parca's
native custom labels, which are independent of whether Go itself is
enabled. Setting only the Go half is the regression that turned up while

## Dictionary sentinels

Every OTLP profiles dictionary table reserves index 0 for a zero value,
so
that an index of `0` reads as "unset" rather than as a reference to the
first real entry. `reset()` only did that for the string table, so the
first real entry of every other table landed at index 0:

| table | what shipped at index 0 |
| --- | --- |
| `link_table` | nothing — the table was empty, which the spec forbids
outright |
| `location_table` | a real location (`Address=0x3e82ca`, lines,
attributes) |
| `stack_table` | a real stack (`LocationIndices=[0..27]`) |
| `attribute_table` | a real attribute (`KeyStrindex=6`) |

`mapping_table` and `function_table` happened not to trip the checker on
the payloads I captured, but they carry the same rule, so they get the
same treatment.

## Sample timestamps

`Build` stamped the flush window, which is when the exporter ran, not
when
the kernel took the samples. A sample read from the perf buffer can
predate
it by tens of milliseconds, and OTLP requires every
`timestamps_unix_nano` to satisfy `time <= ts < time + duration`. The
builder now tracks the batch's timestamp range and widens the window to
cover it.

## Note on `link_table[0]`

The proto comment says the 16/8 zero-filled form SHOULD be preferred
"for
better compatibility with codecs strictly expecting 16/8 byte array
lengths", but `profcheck` compares against a bare `Link{}` with
`proto.Equal`, which a zero-filled one fails. Since we emit no links at
all, this uses the strict zero value; it is commented in place.
